{{Short description|Type of metric in Riemannian geometry}}
{{Use American English|date = March 2019}}
In [[differential geometry]], a '''Kähler–Einstein metric''' on a [[complex manifold]] is a [[Riemannian metric]] that is both a [[Kähler metric]] and an [[Einstein manifold|Einstein metric]].  A [[manifold]] is said to be '''Kähler–Einstein''' if it admits a Kähler–Einstein metric.<ref>Huybrechts 04, Definition 4.B.11</ref>  The most important special case of these are the [[Calabi–Yau manifold]]s, which are Kähler and [[Ricci-flat]].

The most important problem for this area is the existence of Kähler–Einstein metrics for compact Kähler manifolds. This problem can be split up into three cases dependent on the sign of the first [[Chern class]] of the Kähler manifold:

* When the first Chern class is negative, there is always a Kähler–Einstein metric, as [[Thierry Aubin]] and [[Shing-Tung Yau]] proved independently.
* When the first Chern class is zero, there is always a Kähler–Einstein metric, as Yau proved in the [[Calabi conjecture]]. That leads to the name Calabi–Yau manifolds. He was awarded with the [[Fields Medal]] partly because of this work.
* The third case, the positive or Fano case, remained a well-known open problem for many years. In this case, there is a non-trivial obstruction to existence. In 2012, [[Xiuxiong Chen]], [[Simon Donaldson]], and [[Song Sun]] proved that in this case existence is equivalent to an  algebro-geometric criterion called [[K-stability of Fano varieties|K-stability]]. Their proof appeared in a series of articles in the Journal of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref name="CDS1">{{cite journal |s2cid=119641827 |title=Kähler-Einstein metrics on Fano manifolds. I: Approximation of metrics with cone singularities |journal=Journal of the American Mathematical Society |year=2014 |volume=28 |pages=183–197 |doi=10.1090/S0894-0347-2014-00799-2 |arxiv=1211.4566 |last1=Chen |first1=Xiuxiong |last2=Donaldson |first2=Simon |author-link2=Simon Donaldson |last3=Sun |first3=Song}}</ref><ref name="CDS2">{{cite journal |doi=10.1090/S0894-0347-2014-00800-6 |title=Kähler-Einstein metrics on Fano manifolds. II: Limits with cone angle less than 2π |year=2014 |last1=Chen |first1=Xiuxiong |last2=Donaldson |first2=Simon|author-link2=Simon Donaldson |last3=Sun |first3=Song |s2cid=119140033 |journal=Journal of the American Mathematical Society |volume=28 |pages=199–234 |arxiv=1212.4714}}</ref><ref name="CDS3">{{cite journal |doi=10.1090/S0894-0347-2014-00801-8 |title=Kähler-Einstein metrics on Fano manifolds. III: Limits as cone angle approaches 2π and completion of the main proof |year=2014 |last1=Chen |first1=Xiuxiong |last2=Donaldson |first2=Simon |author-link2=Simon Donaldson |last3=Sun |first3=Song |s2cid=119575364 |journal=Journal of the American Mathematical Society |volume=28 |pages=235–278 |arxiv=1302.0282}}</ref> A proof was produced independently by [[Tian Gang|Gang Tian]] at the same time.<ref name=":1" />

When first Chern class is not definite, or we have intermediate Kodaira dimension, then finding canonical metric remained as an open problem, which is called the algebrization conjecture via analytical minimal model program.<!-- This isn't grammatical and I don't understand it enough to fix it. Anybody? -->

==Definition==
===Einstein manifolds===
{{Main article|Einstein manifold}}

Suppose <math>(X,g)</math> is a [[Riemannian manifold]]. In physics the [[Einstein field equations]] are a set of [[partial differential equations]] on the [[metric tensor]] <math>g</math> which describe how the manifold <math>X</math> should curve due to the existence of mass or energy, a quantity encapsulated by the [[stress–energy tensor]] <math>T</math>. In a vacuum where there is no mass or energy, that is <math>T=0</math>, the Einstein Field Equations simplify. Namely, the [[Ricci curvature]] of <math>g</math> is a symmetric <math>(2,0)</math>-tensor, as is the metric <math>g</math> itself, and the equations reduce to

:<math>\operatorname{Ric}_g= \frac{1}{2}R_g g</math>

where <math>R_g</math> is the [[scalar curvature]] of <math>g</math>. That is, the Ricci curvature becomes proportional to the metric. A Riemannian manifold <math>(X,g)</math> satisfying the above equation is called an [[Einstein manifold]].

Every two-dimensional Riemannian manifold is Einstein. It can be proven using the [[Bianchi identities]] that, in any larger dimension, the scalar curvature of any connected Einstein manifold must be constant. For this reason, the Einstein condition is often given as

:<math>\operatorname{Ric}_g= \lambda g</math>

for a real number <math>\lambda.</math>

===Kähler manifolds===
{{Main article|Kähler manifold}}

When the Riemannian manifold <math>(X,g)</math> is also a [[complex manifold]], that is it comes with an integrable [[almost-complex structure]] <math>J:TX\to TX</math>, it is possible to ask for a compatibility between the metric structure <math>g</math> and the complex structure <math>J</math>. There are many equivalent ways of formulating this compatibility condition, and one succinct interpretation is to ask that <math>J</math> is [[orthogonal transformation|orthogonal]] with respect to <math>g</math>, so that <math>g(Ju,Jv)=g(u,v)</math> for all vector fields <math>u,v\in \Gamma(TM)</math>, and that <math>J</math> is preserved by the [[parallel transport]] of the [[Levi-Civita connection]] <math>\nabla</math>, captured by the condition <math>\nabla J = 0</math>. Such a triple <math>(X,g,J)</math> is called a [[Kähler manifold]].

===Kähler–Einstein metrics===

A Kähler–Einstein manifold is one which combines the above properties of being Kähler and admitting an Einstein metric. The combination of these properties implies a simplification of the Einstein equation in terms of the complex structure. Namely, on a Kähler manifold one can define the [[Ricci curvature#Kähler manifolds|Ricci form]], a real [[complex differential form|<math>(1,1)</math>-form]], by the expression

:<math>\rho(u,v) = \operatorname{Ric}_g(Ju,v),</math>
where <math>u,v</math> are any tangent [[vector field]]s to <math>X</math>.

The almost-complex structure <math>J</math> forces <math>\rho</math> to be antisymmetric, and the compatibility condition <math>\nabla J = 0</math> combined with the Bianchi identity implies that <math>\rho</math> is a [[closed differential form]]. Associated to the Riemannian metric <math>g</math> is the [[Kähler form]] <math>\omega</math> defined by a similar expression <math>\omega(u,v)=g(Ju,v)</math>. Therefore the Einstein equations for <math>g</math> can be rewritten as
:<math>\rho = \lambda \omega,</math>
the Kähler–Einstein equation.

Since this is an equality of closed differential forms, it implies an equality of the associated [[de Rham cohomology]] classes <math>[\rho]</math> and <math>[\omega]</math>. The former class is the first [[Chern class]] of <math>X</math>, <math>c_1(X)</math>. Therefore a necessary condition for the existence of a solution to the Kähler–Einstein equation is that <math>\lambda \omega \in c_1(X)</math>, for some <math>\lambda \in \mathbb{R}</math>. This is a topological necessary condition on the Kähler manifold <math>(X,g,J)</math>.

Note that since the Ricci curvature <math>\operatorname{Ric}_g</math> is invariant under scaling <math>g\mapsto \lambda^{-1}g</math>, if there is a metric such that <math>\lambda \omega \in c_1(X)</math>, one can always normalise to a new metric with <math>\omega \in c_1(X)</math>, that is <math>\lambda = -1,0,1</math>. Thus the Kähler–Einstein equation is often written

:<math>\rho = -\omega, \quad \rho = 0,\quad \rho = \omega</math>

depending on the sign of the topological constant <math>\lambda</math>.

==Transformation to a complex Monge–Ampere equation==

The situation of compact Kähler manifolds is special, because the Kähler–Einstein equation can be reformulated as a complex [[Monge–Ampere equation]] for a smooth [[Kähler potential]] on <math>X</math>.<ref name="gabor">{{cite book |first=Gabor |last=Székelyhidi |title=An introduction to extremal Kähler metrics | year=2014 |series=Graduate Studies in Mathematics |volume=152 |publisher=American Mathematical Soc. |isbn=978-1-470-41047-6}}</ref> By the topological assumption on the Kähler manifold, we may always assume that there exists some Kähler metric <math>\omega_0</math> with <math>\lambda\omega_0\in c_1(X)</math>. The Ricci form <math>\rho_0</math> of <math>\omega_0</math> is given in local coordinates by the formula

:<math>\rho_0 = - i \partial \bar \partial \log \omega_0^n.</math>
By assumption <math>\lambda\omega_0</math> and <math>\rho_0</math> are in the same cohomology class <math>c_1(X)</math>, so the [[ddbar lemma|<math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma]] from [[Hodge theory]] implies there exists a smooth function <math>F\in C^{\infty}(X)</math> such that <math>\lambda\omega_0 + i \partial \bar \partial F = \rho_0</math>.

Any other metric <math>\omega\in c_1(X)</math> is related to <math>\omega_0</math> by a [[Kähler potential]] <math>\varphi\in C^{\infty}(X)</math> such that <math>\omega = \omega_0 + i \partial \bar \partial \varphi</math>. It then follows that if <math>\rho</math> is the Ricci form with respect to <math>\omega</math>, then

:<math>\rho - \rho_0 = -i\partial \bar \partial \log \frac{\omega^n}{\omega_0^n}.</math>

Thus to make <math>\rho=\lambda \omega</math> we need to find <math>\varphi</math> such that

:<math>\lambda i\partial \bar\partial \varphi = i \partial \bar \partial F - i \partial \bar \partial \log \frac{\omega^n}{\omega_0^n}.</math>

This will certainly be true if the same equation is proven after removing the derivatives <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>, and in fact this is an equivalent equation by the <math>\partial \bar \partial</math>-lemma up to changing <math>\varphi</math> by the addition of a constant function. In particular, after removing <math>\partial \bar \partial</math> and exponentiating, the equation is transformed into 
:<math>(\omega_0 + i \partial \bar \partial \varphi)^n = e^{F-\lambda \varphi} \omega_0^n.</math>
This [[partial differential equation]] is similar to a real [[Monge–Ampere equation]], and is known as a complex Monge–Ampere equation, and subsequently can be studied using tools from [[convex analysis]]. Its behaviour is highly sensitive to the sign of the topological constant <math>\lambda = -1,0,1</math>. The solutions of this equation appear as critical points of the [[K-energy functional]] introduced by [[Toshiki Mabuchi]] on the space of [[Kähler potential]]s in the class <math>c_1(X)</math>.

==Existence==

The existence problem for Kähler–Einstein metrics can be split up into three distinct cases, dependent on the sign of the topological constant <math>\lambda</math>. Since the Kähler form <math>\omega</math> is always a [[positive form|positive differential form]], the sign of <math>\lambda</math> depends on whether the cohomology class <math>c_1(X)</math> is positive, negative, or zero. In [[algebraic geometry]] this is understood in terms of the [[canonical bundle]] of <math>X</math>: <math>c_1(X)<0</math> if and only if the canonical bundle <math>K_X</math> is an [[ample line bundle]], and <math>c_1(X)>0</math> if and only if <math>K_X^{-1}</math> is ample. If <math>K_X</math> is a trivial line bundle, then <math>c_1(X)=0</math>.
When the Kähler manifold is [[compact manifold|compact]], the problem of existence has been completely solved.

===The case ''c<sub>1</sub>(X)<0''===

When the Kähler manifold <math>X</math> satisfies the topological assumption <math>c_1(X)<0</math>, the canonical bundle is ample and so <math>\lambda</math> must be negative. If the necessary topological assumption is satisfied, that is there exists a Kähler metric <math>\omega</math> such that <math>c_1(X) = \lambda [\omega]</math>, then it was proven by Aubin and Yau that a Kähler–Einstein metric always exists.<ref>{{cite journal |first=T. |last=Aubin |title=Équations du type Monge-Ampère sur les variétés kähleriennes compactes |journal=[[Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Sciences|C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris]] |series=Sér. A-B |volume=283 |issue=3 |pages=Aiii, A119–A121 |year=1976 |doi= }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first=Shing-Tung |last=Yau |authorlink=Shing-Tung Yau |title=Calabi's conjecture and some new results in algebraic geometry |journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]] |volume=74 |issue=5 |pages=1798–1799 |year=1977 |doi= 10.1073/pnas.74.5.1798|pmid=16592394 |pmc=431004 |bibcode=1977PNAS...74.1798Y |doi-access=free }}</ref> The existence of a Kähler metric satisfying the topological assumption is a consequence of Yau's proof of the [[Calabi conjecture]].

<blockquote>'''Theorem (Aubin, Yau):''' A compact Kähler manifold with <math>c_1(X)<0</math> always admits a Kähler–Einstein metric.<ref>Huybrechts 04, Theorem 4.B.24</ref></blockquote>

===The case ''c<sub>1</sub>(X)=0''===
{{See also|Calabi–Yau manifold|Calabi conjecture}}
When the canonical bundle <math>K_X</math> is trivial, so that <math>c_1(X)=0</math>, the manifold is said to be [[Calabi–Yau manifold|Calabi–Yau]]. These manifolds are of special significance in physics, where they should appear as the [[string background]] in [[superstring theory]] in 10 dimensions. Mathematically, this corresponds to the case where <math>\lambda = 0</math>, that is, when the Riemannian manifold <math>(X,g)</math> is [[Ricci flat]].

The existence of a Kähler–Einstein metric was proven in this case by Yau, using a continuity method similar to the case where <math>c_1(X)<0</math>.<ref>[[Shing-Tung Yau]]. On the Ricci curvature of a compact Kähler manifold and the complex Monge-Ampère equation. I. [[Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics]], 31(3):339–411, 1978.</ref> The topological assumption <math>c_1(X)=0</math> introduces new difficulties into the continuity method. Partly due to his proof of existence, and the related proof of the [[Calabi conjecture]], Yau was awarded the [[Fields Medal]].

<blockquote>'''Theorem (Yau):''' A compact Kähler manifold with trivial canonical bundle, a Calabi–Yau manifold, always admits a Kähler–Einstein metric, and in particular admits a Ricci-flat metric.</blockquote>

===The case ''c<sub>1</sub>(X)>0''===

{{See also|Fano manifold|K-stability|K-stability of Fano varieties}}

When the anticanonical bundle <math>K_X^{-1}</math> is ample, or equivalently <math>c_1(X)>0</math>, the manifold is said to be Fano. In contrast to the case <math>c_1(X)\le 0</math>, a Kähler–Einstein metric does not always exist in this case. It was observed by [[Akito Futaki]] that there are possible obstructions to the existence of a solution given by the [[holomorphic tangent bundle|holomorphic vector field]]s of <math>X</math>, and it is a necessary condition that the [[Futaki invariant]] of these vector fields is non-negative.<ref>{{cite journal |first=A. |last=Futaki |title=An obstruction to the existence of Einstein Kähler metrics |journal=Invent. Math. |volume=73 |year=1983 |issue=3 |pages=437–443 |doi=10.1007/BF01388438 |bibcode=1983InMat..73..437F |s2cid=121382431 }}</ref> Indeed, much earlier it had been observed by Matsushima and Lichnerowicz that another necessary condition is that the Lie algebra of holomorphic vector fields <math>H^0(X,TX)</math> must be [[reductive Lie algebra|reductive]].<ref>{{cite journal |first=Yozo |last=Matsushima |authorlink=Yozo Matsushima |title=Sur la structure du groupe d'homéomorphismes analytiques d'une certaine variété kählérienne |journal=Nagoya Math. J. |volume=11 |issue= |pages=145–150 |year=1957 |doi=10.1017/S0027763000002026 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |first=André |last=Lichnerowicz |authorlink=André Lichnerowicz |title=Géométrie des groupes de transformations |series=Travaux et Recherches Mathématiques |volume=III |publisher=Dunod |location=Paris |year=1958 }}</ref>

It was conjectured by Yau in 1993, in analogy with the similar problem of existence of [[Hermite–Einstein metric]]s on [[holomorphic vector bundle]]s, that the obstruction to existence of a Kähler–Einstein metric should be equivalent to a certain [[algebraic geometry|algebro-geometric]] stability condition similar to [[Stable vector bundle|slope stability]] of vector bundles.<ref>{{cite book |first=S.-T. |last=Yau |chapter=Open problems in geometry |title=Differential geometry: partial differential equations on manifolds (Los Angeles, CA, 1990) |volume=54 |series=Proc. Sympos. Pure Math. |pages=1–28 |publisher=Amer. Math. Soc. |location=Providence, RI |year=1993 |isbn=0-8218-1494-X }}</ref> In 1997 [[Gang Tian|Tian Gang]] proposed a possible stability condition, which came to be known as [[K-stability of Fano varieties|K-stability]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Tian|first=Gang|author-link=Tian Gang|year=1997|title=Kähler-Einstein metrics with positive scalar curvature|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s002220050176|journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]]|volume=130|issue=1|pages=1–37|doi=10.1007/s002220050176|bibcode=1997InMat.130....1T|mr=1471884|s2cid=122529381|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The conjecture of Yau was resolved in 2012 by [[Xiuxiong Chen|Chen]]–[[Simon Donaldson|Donaldson]]–[[Song Sun|Sun]] using techniques largely different from the classical continuity method of the case <math>c_1(X)\le 0</math>,<ref name="CDS1" /><ref name="CDS2" /><ref name="CDS3" /> and at the same time by Tian.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal |last=Tian |first=G. |year=2015 |title=K-stability and Kähler–Einstein metrics |journal=Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics |volume=68 |issue=7 |pages=1085–1156 |doi=10.1002/cpa.21578 |arxiv=1211.4669 |s2cid=119303358 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Tian |first=G. |title=Corrigendum: K-stability and Kähler–Einstein metrics |journal=Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics |volume=68 |issue=11 |pages=2082–2083 |year=2015 |doi=10.1002/cpa.21612 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Chen–Donaldson–Sun have disputed Tian's proof, claiming that it contains mathematical inaccuracies and material which should be attributed to them.{{efn|Xiuxiong Chen, Simon Donaldson, Song Sun. [https://wwwf.imperial.ac.uk/~skdona/KEDEVELOPMENTS-9-19-2013.PDF "On some recent developments in Kähler geometry."]}} Tian has disputed these claims.{{efn|Gang Tian. [http://tian.bicmr.pku.edu.cn/Documents_on_K_hler_Geometry.htm "Response to CDS" and "More comments on CDS."], [https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/cpa.21612 Corrigendum: K-Stability and Kähler‐Einstein Metrics]}} The 2019 [[Veblen prize]] was awarded to Chen–Donaldson–Sun for their proof.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/news?news_id=4705|title=2019 Oswald Veblen Prize in Geometry to Xiuxiong Chen, Simon Donaldson, and Song Sun|date=2018-11-19|website=American Mathematical Society|access-date=2019-04-09}}</ref> Donaldson was awarded the 2015 [[Breakthrough Prize in Mathematics]] in part for his contribution to the proof,<ref>[https://breakthroughprize.org/Laureates/L55 Simon Donaldson "For the new revolutionary invariants of four-dimensional manifolds and for the study of the relation between stability in algebraic geometry and in global differential geometry, both for bundles and for Fano varieties."]</ref> and the 2021 [[Breakthrough Prize in Mathematics#New Horizons in Mathematics Prize|New Horizons Breakthrough Prize]] was awarded to Sun in part for his contribution.<ref>[https://breakthroughprize.org/News/60 Breakthrough Prize in Mathematics 2021]</ref>

<blockquote>'''Theorem:''' A compact Fano manifold <math>X</math> admits a Kähler–Einstein metric if and only if the pair <math>(X,K_X^{-1})</math> is K-polystable.</blockquote>
A proof based along the lines of the continuity method which resolved the case <math>c_1(X)\le 0</math> was later provided by Datar–Székelyhidi, and several other proofs are now known.<ref>{{cite journal |first=G. |last=Székelyhidi |title=The partial <math>C^0</math>-estimate along the continuity method |journal=J. Amer. Math. Soc. |volume=29 |year=2016 |pages=537–560 |doi=10.1090/jams/833 |arxiv=1310.8471 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first1=V. |last1=Datar |first2=G. |last2=Székelyhidi |title=Kähler–Einstein metrics along the smooth continuity method |journal=Geom. Funct. Anal. |volume=26 |year=2016 |issue=4 |pages=975–1010 |doi=10.1007/s00039-016-0377-4 |arxiv=1506.07495 |s2cid=118246980 }}</ref> See the [[K-stability#Yau–Tian–Donaldson Conjecture|Yau–Tian–Donaldson conjecture]] for more details.

==Kähler–Ricci flow and the minimal model program==

A central program in [[birational geometry]] is the [[minimal model program]], which seeks to generate models of [[algebraic varieties]] inside every birationality class, which are in some sense ''minimal'', usually in that they minimize certain measures of complexity (such as the [[arithmetic genus]] in the case of curves). In higher dimensions, one seeks a minimal model which has [[Nef line bundle|''nef'' canonical bundle]]. One way to construct minimal models is to contract certain curves <math>C\subset X</math> inside an algebraic variety <math>X</math> which have negative self-intersection. These curves should be thought of geometrically as subvarieties on which <math>X</math> has a concentration of negative curvature.

In this sense, the minimal model program can be viewed as an analogy of the [[Ricci flow]] in differential geometry, where regions where curvature concentrate are expanded or contracted in order to reduce the original Riemannian manifold to one with uniform curvature (precisely, to a new Riemannian manifold which has uniform Ricci curvature, which is to say an Einstein manifold). In the case of 3-manifolds, this was famously used by [[Grigori Perelman]] to prove the [[Poincaré conjecture]].

In the setting of Kähler manifolds, the '''Kähler–Ricci flow''' was first written down by Cao.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Cao |first=Huai-Dong |title=Deformation of Kähler matrics to Kähler-Einstein metrics on compact Kähler manifolds |journal=Inventiones Mathematicae |volume=81 |year=1985 |issue=2 |pages=359–372 |doi=10.1007/BF01389058 |bibcode=1985InMat..81..359C |s2cid=124733796 }}</ref> Here one fixes a Kähler metric <math>g_{i\bar j}</math> with Ricci form <math>\rho_{i\bar j}</math>, and studies the [[geometric flow]] for a family of Kähler metrics <math>\tilde{g}_{ij}(t)</math> parametrised by <math>t\in [0,\infty)</math>:
:<math>\frac{\partial \tilde{g}_{i\bar j}}{\partial t} = -\tilde{\rho}_{i\bar j} + \rho_{i\bar j},\quad \tilde{g}_{i\bar j}(0) = g_{i\bar j}.</math>
When a [[projective variety]] <math>X</math> is of [[Kodaira dimension|general type]], the minimal model <math>X'</math> admits a further simplification to a ''canonical model'' <math>X''</math>, with ample canonical bundle. In settings where there are only mild ([[orbifold]]) singularities to this canonical model, it is possible to ask whether the Kähler–Ricci flow of <math>X</math> converges to a (possibly mildly singular) Kähler–Einstein metric on <math>X''</math>, which should exist by Yau and Aubin's existence result for <math>c_1(X'')<0</math>.

A precise result along these lines was proven by Cascini and La Nave,<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Cascini |first1=P. |last2=La Nave |first2=G. |year=2006 |title=Kähler-Ricci Flow and the Minimal Model Program for Projective Varieties |eprint=math/0603064 }}</ref> and around the same time by Tian–Zhang.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tian |first1=G. |last2=Zhang |first2=Z. |year=2006 |title=On the Kähler–Ricci flow on projective manifolds of general type |journal=Chinese Annals of Mathematics, Series B |volume=27 |issue=2 |pages=179–192 |doi=10.1007/s11401-005-0533-x |s2cid=16476473 }}</ref>
<blockquote>'''Theorem:''' The Kähler–Ricci flow on a projective variety <math>X</math> of general type exists for all time, and after at most a finite number of singularity formations, if the canonical model <math>X''</math> of <math>X</math> has at worst orbifold singularities, then the Kähler–Ricci flow on <math>X</math> converges to the Kähler–Einstein metric on <math>X''</math>, up to a bounded function which is smooth away from an analytic subvariety of <math>X</math>.</blockquote>
In the case where the variety <math>X</math> is of dimension two, so is a surface of general type, one gets convergence to the 
Kähler–Einstein metric on <math>X''</math>.

Later, Jian Song and Tian studied the case where the projective variety <math>X</math> has log-terminal singularities.<ref name="songtian">{{cite arXiv |eprint=0909.4898 |last1=Song |first1=Jian |last2=Tian |first2=Gang |author-link2=Gang Tian |title=The Kahler-Ricci flow through singularities |year=2009 |class=math.DG }}</ref>

===Kähler–Ricci flow and existence of Kähler–Einstein metrics===

It is possible to give an alternative proof of the Chen–Donaldson–Sun theorem on existence of Kähler–Einstein metrics on a smooth Fano manifold using the Kähler-Ricci flow, and this was carried out in 2018 by Chen–Sun–Wang.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Xiuxiong |last1=Chen |first2=Song |last2=Sun |first3=Bing |last3=Wang |title=Kähler–Ricci flow, Kähler–Einstein metric, and K–stability |journal=Geom. Topol. |volume=2 |issue=6 |pages=3145–3173 |year=2018 |doi=10.2140/gt.2018.22.3145 |arxiv=1508.04397 |s2cid=5667938 }}</ref> Namely, if the Fano manifold is K-polystable, then the Kähler-Ricci flow exists for all time and converges to a Kähler–Einstein metric on the Fano manifold.

==Generalizations and alternative notions==

===Constant scalar curvature Kähler metrics===

{{Main article|Constant scalar curvature Kähler metric}}
When the canonical bundle <math>K_X</math> is not trivial, ample, or anti-ample, it is not possible to ask for a Kähler–Einstein metric, as the class <math>c_1(X)</math> cannot contain a Kähler metric, and so the necessary topological condition can never be satisfied. This follows from the [[Kodaira embedding theorem]].

A natural generalisation of the Kähler–Einstein equation to the more general setting of an arbitrary compact Kähler manifold is to ask that the Kähler metric has constant [[scalar curvature]] (one says the metric is '''cscK'''). The scalar curvature is the total trace of the [[Riemannian curvature tensor]], a smooth function on the manifold <math>(X,g)</math>, and in the Kähler case the condition that the scalar curvature is constant admits a transformation into an equation similar to the complex Monge–Ampere equation of the Kähler–Einstein setting. Many techniques from the Kähler–Einstein case carry on to the cscK setting, albeit with added difficulty, and it is [[K-stability#Yau–Tian–Donaldson Conjecture|conjectured]] that a similar algebro-geometric stability condition should imply the existence of solutions to the equation in this more general setting.

When the compact Kähler manifold satisfies the topological assumptions necessary for the Kähler–Einstein condition to make sense, the constant scalar curvature Kähler equation reduces to the Kähler–Einstein equation.

===Hermite–Einstein metrics===

{{Main article|Hermitian Yang–Mills connection}}
Instead of asking the Ricci curvature of the Levi-Civita connection on the [[tangent bundle]] of a Kähler manifold <math>X</math> is proportional to the metric itself, one can instead ask this question for the curvature of a [[Chern connection]] associated to a [[Hermitian metric]] on ''any'' [[holomorphic vector bundle]] over <math>X</math> (note that the Levi-Civita connection on the holomorphic tangent bundle is precisely the Chern connection of the Hermitian metric coming from the Kähler structure). The resulting equation is called the Hermite–Einstein equation, and is of special importance in [[gauge theory (mathematics)|gauge theory]], where it appears as a special case of the [[Yang–Mills equations]], which come from [[quantum field theory]], in contrast to the regular Einstein equations which come from [[general relativity]].

In the case where the holomorphic vector bundle is again the [[holomorphic tangent bundle]] and the Hermitian metric is the 
Kähler metric, the Hermite–Einstein equation reduces to the Kähler–Einstein equation. In general however, the geometry of the Kähler manifold is often fixed and only the bundle metric is allowed to vary, and this causes the Hermite–Einstein equation to be easier to study than the Kähler–Einstein equation in general. In particular, a complete algebro-geometric characterisation of the existence of solutions is given by the [[Kobayashi–Hitchin correspondence]].
